title: Local Perceptions and Practices of News Sharing and Fake News
screen_reason: Online survey of 75 Singapore-based respondents. A branching question split off the 57 respondents 'who said that they have come across fake news before', giving a verbatim part/whole share of the same denominator (57 of 75 = 76.0%) — a RECALL exposure estimate. The paper also reports, among those 57, the media where fake news was observed (instant messaging apps 77.2%, social media 70.2%, word-of-mouth 66.7%), which are further recall-exposure shares (conditional on prior exposure).

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own judgement that a news item they encountered was fake; no external verification. The authors themselves flag this as unresolved: 'it will be of interest to see what news people consider as "fake" in Singapore'.
estimates.moderator_quote: The survey was written in English and made available to anyone with the hyperlink. Participation was fully voluntary. For dissemination, various channels were employed including a mailing list of students from a local Singapore university, an informal Telegram supergroup joined by students, alumni, and faculty of the same university, and personal contacts of the researchers. Further spreading of the survey by participants was encouraged.
estimates.notes: The 76.0% is not printed as a percentage anywhere; it is the exact part/whole share of two verbatim counts with the same denominator (57 of SG-75's 75), which R8 permits. The paper never frames it as a prevalence estimate — the split exists only to define the SeenFake-57 analysis subset. Heavily skewed convenience sample: 58 of 75 are students and 48 of 75 are aged 18-24, recruited largely through one university's mailing list and Telegram group, with snowballing encouraged; all respondents are by construction digitally proficient (acknowledged by the authors). No time window is attached to 'before', so this is a lifetime-ever measure. missed_or_uncertain: (1) Figure 1 reports fake-news source percentages for all 11 media items but only the top three are given numerically in the text; the remaining eight could not be read off a figure that is not in this text file. (2) '50.9% (n = 29) sent a correction message to those whom they have shared the news with' implies those respondents had themselves shared the fake news, and could be read as a recall-SHARING share of SeenFake-57. I did not extract it: the item measures an action taken after realising news was fake, not a direct question about having shared misinformation, and a respondent could plausibly answer for news they forwarded before knowing its status or interpret 'shared' loosely. An adjudicator may wish to overrule this. (3) 'SharedNews-59' (59 of 75 = 78.7%) is about sharing NEWS generally, not misinformation, so it is out of scope. (4) All Likert results (fake news will remain M = 4.33; harmful M = 4.42; sharing a greater problem than creation M = 3.93 vs 3.54; awareness among the general populace M = 2.74; trust before M = 3.56 vs after M = 2.88; trust in the 11 media items) are scale means with no share of respondents above a threshold, so no rows per the exclusion for means-only. (5) News-sharing motivations and verification habits (relevant 89.8%, always verify 25.4%, frequently verify 47.5%, etc.) are behaviours around news generally, not misinformation exposure or sharing. (6) Speed-of-realisation figures (very soon 33.3%, within the day 42.1%) and tools used (search engine 86.0%) describe detection behaviour, not prevalence. (7) DATE JUDGEMENT CALL: the data-collection period is nowhere stated. year = 2020 is inferred from the first arXiv posting (2010.07607, October 2020), which bounds collection at or before 2020; the Scopus record and the v2 reference list (retrieved June 2021) point to 2021 as the publication year. An adjudicator may prefer year = 2021.

rob.design: Voluntary online survey in English, open to anyone with the link, disseminated through a Singapore university student mailing list, an informal Telegram supergroup of students/alumni/faculty of that university, and the researchers' personal contacts, with onward sharing encouraged (snowball). 104 responses received; 75 met the criterion of being currently based in Singapore (SG-75). Instrument: 19 question items, 2 branching questions, 3 demographic questions, covering 11 traditional and digital media items; branching routed respondents so that each answered question rested on their own experience, creating SharedNews-59 (n = 59) and SeenFake-57 (n = 57). IRB approved by the authors' university. No response rate is computable for an open link; no weighting; sample skews young (48/75 aged 18-24) and student (58/75 students, 13 employed). No external verification of what respondents counted as 'fake news'; all measures are self-report. Analysis reported: Friedman test on trust across the 11 media (chi-square(10) = 338, p < .0001) and a correlation between media source of fake news and trust (r(9) = -0.81, p < .005).
